data.title: Uncovering the secrets of ancient Rome on the Middle Danube
data.excerpt: A weekend along the Roman frontier of the Middle Danube: the fort at Iža opposite the legionary fortress of Brigetio, the Roman lapidarium in Komárno, Carnuntum in Lower Austria and the newly opened archaeopark at Cífer – Pác. On the way, the piers of a Roman bridge sought in the bed of the Danube, the Heidentor that is neither a gate nor pagan, and a Germanic magnate’s court with under-floor heating.

children.text: It is the holidays, and during the holidays we somehow find time more often for trips lasting several days. Our steps, as in past summers, led to the rivers; this time they led to the Danube. We packed a tent and sleeping bags, a billy can for the morning coffee, and set off on our way.

Over the weekend we visited the Roman camp in the village of Iža in Slovakia, the Roman lapidarium in the town of Komárno, Carnuntum in Lower Austria, and at the end we did not want to miss a visit to the newly opened archaeopark in Cífer - Pác.
The Roman camp at Iža

The village of Iža lies close to the Danube, in the southernmost part of Slovakia and in the easternmost projection of the Danubian Plain. The area is an important archaeological site with evidence of occupation as early as the Stone Age. Among the tourist attractions near the village are the remains of the Roman camp, whose name has commonly become established among the public as Kelemantia, and the Bokrošské slanisko nature reserve. Archaeological finds in the basin of the Danube prove that this territory was already inhabited in the Stone Age. It became an even more inhabited territory when, at the end of the tenth millennium BC, the last Ice Age came to an end and the climate came to resemble that of today. People sought out territories suitable for their livelihood, such as valleys in river basins and fertile fields, where they settled and gradually began to cultivate the soil. Alongside hunting and fishing they began to till the land and to keep animals, as a result of which they became tied to a particular territory. In this way a certain form of agriculture came into being. In a territory where they had favourable conditions for making a living they settled for a longer time. The finds testify that this was an ancient agricultural territory. From the 2nd millennium onwards the production of bronze gradually spread across central Europe and various crafts flourished. Thanks to this, various social and property classes also began to form. In the later Bronze Age the typical Danubian culture arose which we know under the name “limestone-encrusted pottery”.

blocks.caption: Fig.: a shot from the orthophoto map of 1950
blocks.alt: Fig.: a shot from the orthophoto map of 1950

children.text: In the earlier Iron Age, in the years 700–400 BC, Thracian tribes came to this territory from the eastern part of the Carpathian Basin, which is proved by the find of an extensive cemetery at Chotín. In the 4th century BC Celtic tribes migrated into the territory of the present-day Danubian Lowland. Their arrival meant perhaps the greatest turning point in ancient history. They were masters of various crafts, above all smithing and glassmaking, and they excelled in pottery production and in the making of hand mills. The development of craft production was secured above all by the invention of iron smelting. In agriculture they began genuine cultivation of the soil. A great development of trade came when they were the first in this territory to strike coins and to use them as a means of payment for goods. They lived in tribes, in which the family played an important role.

The ruling class arose from the wealthier stratum; they were aristocrats who were able to control a considerably differentiated Celtic society. They built dwelling houses in homesteads, rectangular in shape and measuring 3 × 5 metres. These they built below ground level. At the turn of the last century BC the united tribes of the Dacians subjugated the Celts.

In the 1st century AD the territory of present-day south-western Slovakia, settled by the tribes of the Germanic Marcomanni and Quadi, lay in direct proximity to the Roman Empire. The natural northern frontier of the empire – of the province of Pannonia – was formed in this area by the Danube, along which the Romans gradually built an extensive frontier fortress system, the so-called LIMES ROMANUS, which consisted of military camps. The military fortress at Iža was part of it as well.
At the beginning of the 5th century the tribes of the Huns came to the Carpathian Basin from Central Asia.
At the beginning of the 6th century the Slavs began to populate the Carpathian Basin, settling mainly in the river basins and on the hills.

In the second half of the 6th century the Avars came into the area. They were a warlike people who also subjugated the left bank of the Danube. In the neighbouring villages of Radvaň nad Dunajom, Žitava and Virt archaeologists have uncovered their cemeteries. In Komárno eight Avar cemeteries were found. The Avars lived in tribes whose core was formed by the members of a single clan. They frequently threatened the Slavs. Their dominance ended at the close of the 8th century, when they suffered a fateful defeat at the hands of the Frankish ruler Charlemagne.

At the end of the 9th century the Hungarian tribes came to the Carpathian Basin and gradually populated this countryside. Their traces are found at Nesvady, Marcelová, Chotín, Svätý Peter, Imeľ, Bátorove Kosihy, Zlatná na Ostrove and Zemianska Olča.

The dwelling settlements created in early feudalism later served for the founding of larger settlements and for the emergence of towns and villages, mainly in the 13th century, when the greatest flourishing of feudalism followed.

children.text: From the cultural and historical point of view the most important military camp in the territory of Slovakia is the Leányvár (Maiden’s Castle) at Iža. Claudius Ptolemy, who was the first to describe the geography of the world of his day in text and in figures, already mentions a trading settlement named Celemantia in the area north of the Danube. The Roman military camp, however, came into being only after his death, so Ptolemy could not have been referring to the Roman military camp at which archaeological excavation is being carried out today. The name Celemantia was adopted by historians much later, only in the first half of the 20th century, and this designation survives among the general public to this day. The archaeological excavation at Iža, which began in 1978 (the directors of the excavation: doc. PhDr. Klára Kuzmová, CSc. and PhDr. Ján Rajtár, CSc.), has cast doubt on the view that this is the Celemantia mentioned by Ptolemy. The greatest credit for our knowledge of the fortress goes to a native of Iža, the archaeologist Dr. János Tóth Kurucz, who by his painstaking work laid the foundations for further research.

blocks.caption: a reconstruction of the fortification and the entrance gateway on the southern side of the camp at Iža
blocks.alt: a reconstruction of the fortification and the entrance gateway on the southern side of the camp at Iža

children.text: Let us return, however, to the Roman period and to the fort at Iža. The Roman military camp near Iža (the locality of Leányvár) was part of the frontier fortification of the Roman Empire from the time of the Marcomannic Wars (c. 175) until the last decades of the 4th century AD. The camp lay on the northern bank of the Danube, opposite the legionary fortress of Brigetio. The ground plan of the stone fort had internal dimensions of 172 × 172 m; its fortification and the layout of its internal buildings correspond to the construction of stone Roman forts in the 2nd and 3rd centuries. The southern front of its fortification was built close to the bank of the Danube, and on sketches of the situation from the 18th century two lines protecting the riverside zone beside the camp were still visible (Kubitschek 1931, 203; Pococke 1743, 245). The Roman fortress at Iža was a strategically advanced place of the Limes Romanus/Ripa Pannonica within the defensive system.
The width of the Danube at Komárno is around 500 metres. This width may change slightly depending on the current water level and on local geographical conditions.

The find of the piers of the bridge which connected Brigetio with the military camp on the opposite bank of the Danube is one of the interesting archaeological discoveries of the period of the Roman Empire. The find spot of the bridge piers lies near the present-day town of Komárno and was an important point on the map of the Roman Empire.

blocks.caption: The bank of the Danube at the spot in front of the gateway of the fortification at Iža
blocks.alt: The bank of the Danube at the spot in front of the gateway of the fortification at Iža

children.text: A bridge over the Danube connecting the banks at Brigetio would probably have been part of the extensive military and commercial system of the Roman Empire, through which important points on the Danube were linked. Archaeological finds in this area include remains of the structure of the bridge, for example wooden piles. Research in the waters of the Danube is demanding. The watercourse has a strong current and, moreover, visibility is sometimes zero, at best 20 cm. In winter visibility is better and the current in the river is also weaker, thanks to the fact that the water is locked up in snow and ice. Thanks to the use of modern sonar, the members of the team of specialists have managed, despite the demanding environment, to record several structures in the river connected with Roman activities in this area.

These archaeological discoveries are important for understanding the history and the technology of Roman building, as well as for the study of the history of the central European region during the Roman period. The construction of such a bridge in an area that was part of the province of Pannonia, at a time when Roman military and trade routes crossed the Danube, may testify to a stable situation on the frontier and to a firm frontier line.

If a functioning bridge had been built at this place, it could have served not only for the movement of military units, which were key to maintaining control and security on the frontier of the Roman Empire, known as the limes.

What dimensions such a bridge could have had is the subject of research. For the bridge to be functional, it would have to be wide enough to allow the passage of Roman legionaries and military wagons. This research seems to be at its beginning, and new insights and results of the research will certainly reveal much more to us in the period to come.

blocks.caption: The Roman fort at Iža
blocks.alt: The Roman fort at Iža

children.text: Roman bridges were usually constructed so as to bear a considerable load and to have sufficient width for various kinds of traffic, which was essential for the effective management and administration of the empire.

We do not yet know of any written mentions of the particular bridge which connected Brigetio and the military camp on the opposite bank of the watercourse. Most of the information about this bridge comes from archaeological finds and from research in the area, not from surviving textual sources.
Archaeological finds such as the remains of the bridge piers, of structural elements and traces of Roman roads provide the most information about the construction of the bridge.

blocks.alt: Danuvina Alacris

children.text: This place attracted great attention in the summer of 2022, when a replica of the Roman oared ship Danuvina Alacris was moored on the bank of the Danube beside the Roman camp near Iža. (you can read more about this ship, and about the voyage on the Budapest – Baja stretch, here:

Voyage on a Roman ship down the Danube – part 2
and
Danuvina Alacris again on the waters of the Danube

At this point I should like to thank doc. Mgr. Miroslava Daňová PhD. of the Department of Classical Archaeology, Faculty of Arts of the University of Trnava in Trnava, who found time for us during our stay at the camp at Iža and showed us round the camp. Her account of the camp, of the excavation and of the finds was instructive and very enjoyable. We look forward to our next meeting.
Brigetio

On the opposite bank of the Danube lay the Roman camp of Brigetio. This military camp is more important than the camp on the Slovak side of the Danube. The military camp on the Hungarian side of the Danube was also considerably larger, and it was built earlier as well. In the surroundings of Brigetio aerial survey has also come upon traces indicating a large number of more recent camps used for short periods of time. From the air only the ditches of the camps are visible, nothing else.

blocks.caption: The Komárno lapidarium
blocks.alt: The Komárno lapidarium

blocks.caption: The Komárno lapidarium
blocks.alt: The Komárno lapidarium

children.text: Their Roman origin cannot, however, be doubted, because they are in the shape of regular rectangles and their corners are smoothly rounded, as is also clear from the forms that are evident for camps of Roman origin of this kind. It is possible, indeed probable, that there were more than the 33 camps in this area that have so far been identified on the Hungarian side. The large number of camps discovered caused surprise and a certain degree of incomprehension. These camps built on the Hungarian as well as on the Slovak side of the Danube were evidently used only for a short time. The Roman military camp of Brigetio, situated in the area of present-day Komárom/Szőny in Hungary, fulfilled from the 2nd century onwards, for more than 300 years, the defensive function of the Roman province of Pannonia, more precisely the protection of the northern frontier, the Ripa Pannonica.

blocks.caption: The ground plan of a classic Roman camp
blocks.alt: The ground plan of a classic Roman camp

children.text: The camps observed on aerial photographs were connected with the Marcomannic Wars of Marcus Aurelius (166–180). Archaeological excavation has also revealed the remains of a representative building near the legionary fortress in which Valentinian I died on 17 November 375, and where his son was proclaimed emperor. The main parts of the complex were the legionary fortress and the military and civilian towns.

The legionary fortress of Brigetio, measuring 540 × 430 m, was built by the legio XI Claudia and then by the legio I Adiutrix in the time of the emperor Trajan (98–117). Its army, consisting of 5,500 men, remained at Brigetio until the 430s, when the province was given up. During archaeological excavations and geophysical survey several important elements of the fortress were identified: the northern gateway (porta praetoria) and the headquarters (principia) of the fortress, the camp hospital (valetudinarium), the baths (thermae), the buildings for storing grain (horrea) and a significant part of its road system.

blocks.caption: The Komárno lapidarium, part of the exhibitions of the Danubian Museum in Komárno
blocks.alt: The Komárno lapidarium, part of the exhibitions of the Danubian Museum in Komárno

children.text: In the course of our journey we also stopped in the town of Komárno. An interesting Roman lapidarium is installed in one of the bastions of the fortress, and it is worth visiting. Besides original Roman stone altars, stone tablets and sarcophagi, you will also find here copies of Roman inscriptions, for example the well-known one from the Trenčín rock.
Besides a pleasant cooling-off on a hot summer day, we took away from there interesting books full of facts at a really good price.

blocks.caption: The Komárno lapidarium
blocks.alt: The Komárno lapidarium

children.text: Carnuntum

Our next steps led westwards. The former capital of the province of Pannonia was a true jewel on the bank of the Danube. Even today it astonishes by its size and by the splendour of its finds. Carnuntum was a bastion on the Danubian stretch of the Roman fortifications against incursions by barbarians, directly on the frontier of the Roman Empire; in the immediate vicinity of a busy trade artery - the Amber Road - it acquired an exceptional strategic, political and economic importance.

blocks.caption: The Roman city quarter of Carnuntum – Villa Urbana
blocks.alt: The Roman city quarter of Carnuntum – Villa Urbana

children.text: The village of Petronell-Carnuntum is a picturesque little Austrian village with a small church and a charming manor house. Today an unremarkable wine-growing village at first glance, in the Roman period it was an important centre of trade and power. In recent years research work has been resumed in the locality of the garden beside the museum, where the forefield of the auxiliary fort was situated. At the very beginning there was the establishment of a temporary winter camp for legionaries – and the small military camp between the 1st and the 4th century AD grew to such an extent that it became the capital of the Roman province of Upper Pannonia, with 50,000 inhabitants. Besides the legionary camp in the middle of the territory of the military town, a pulsating civilian town (municipium) flourished in the territory outside the military zone.

The frontier in the north of the Roman Empire, the Limes Romanus, was closed by the Danube. The importance of Carnuntum did not lie only in its strategic position for the protection of the frontiers of the Roman empire; it became an important metropolis thanks to the close proximity of important trade routes.

blocks.caption: Therme – the baths in the Villa Urbana - Carnuntum
blocks.alt: Therme – the baths in the Villa Urbana - Carnuntum

children.text: From 2005 to 2007 an archaeological excavation of the park in the so-called “villa Urbana” in the north-eastern part of “Insula VI” of the civilian town was carried out. In the present-day village of Petronell-Carnuntum and its surroundings we can visit monuments of the period of the Roman Empire such as the amphitheatre, the Roman city quarter, a magnificent museum and the Heidentor – the Pagan Gate. The Pagan Gate is in fact not a gate, nor is it pagan — it is a triumphal arch in front of the walls of the civilian town.

blocks.caption: An original street in Carnuntum
blocks.alt: An original street in Carnuntum

children.text: The Gate of the Pagans - the Heidentor, situated about 900 m south of the Roman city quarter of Carnuntum, was built by the city most probably during the reign of the emperor Constantius II (Constantius II, AD 337–361). Originally it is a monument in the form of a quadrifrons (a four-gated arch) with double gateways between four piers. The external dimensions formed a “cube” with sides 14.5 metres long. The massive pedestal for a statue in the middle recalls the significance of the monument as a triumphal arch, but because of it passage beneath the arch was not possible. On the pedestal, about 4.3 m high, there probably stood a larger-than-life statue of the emperor.

blocks.caption: Heidentor – the Pagan Gate
blocks.alt: Heidentor – the Pagan Gate

children.text: In the civilian town there was a forum, several temples, a curia, the municipal archive (tabularium), several bath buildings (thermae), insulae and streets. Beside the town stood the civilian amphitheatre with a capacity of 14,000 spectators, dating from the first half of the 2nd century, and next to it a gladiator school (discovered in 2011). From the end of the 2nd century town walls and several luxurious buildings were added. The civilian amphitheatre probably came to an end in the 4th century, because features of this period were found in its southern entrance which suggest that a Christian baptistery probably stood here.
In 308 or 309 several Roman emperors met at Carnuntum under the leadership of the former emperor
Diocletian
at a conference which was to solve the problem of several simultaneous emperors in power (Diocletian,
Galerius
Maximianus
). The meeting, however, did not end successfully, and the struggles for the throne continued in the Roman Empire until the emperor
Constantine the Great
(Constantinus) once again became the sole emperor in the empire.

blocks.caption: The entrance to the therme – the baths in Carnuntum
blocks.alt: The entrance to the therme – the baths in Carnuntum

children.text: In the
4th century
the occupation at Carnuntum began to decline. As a result of the threat to the Danubian frontier from Germanic tribes, a large part of the civilian population moved to the western provinces (Italy,
Gaul
). In the middle of the 4th century the town was struck by an earthquake.
In
the emperor
Valentinian I
, in the course of a campaign against the
Quadi
and the
Sarmatians
, found the town already in ruins, but had the camp rebuilt. The last garrison left Carnuntum probably at the end of the 4th century. The late Roman historian
Ammianus Marcellinus
writes of the town "as a deserted and dirty hole".
Austrian archaeologists have been carrying out excavations on the site of Carnuntum since the end of the
19th century

(perhaps already from the middle of the 19th century), and to date about 3/4 of the town and of the military camp have been uncovered. At the time of our visit, too, preparatory work for archaeological excavation was under way in the complex.
The Cífer – Pác archaeopark

Our last stop on our journey in search of ancient monuments in the surroundings of the Danube was the village of Cífer. The village of Cífer lies in a region that is among the most densely settled regions of Slovakia. The watercourses of the Gidra and the Ronava, together with the most fertile soil in genetic terms, above all chernozem on loess, created an environment ideal for human life. The great density of occupation shows that in the past this area also had strategic importance, and it is very likely that key routes passed through it. So it was not by chance that it was precisely here that the first farmers settled, that the Roman legions built their camps, that a court was built for the Germanic nobility, and that the Slavs and the Avars founded their settlements and cemeteries. The occupation was of differing intensity in different periods. This may also be connected with the continuously changing climatic conditions.

blocks.caption: Archaeopark Cífer - Pác
blocks.alt: Archaeopark Cífer - Pác

blocks.caption: The exhibitions in the Cífer - Pác archaeopark
blocks.alt: The exhibitions in the Cífer - Pác archaeopark

children.text: The largest excavation in this village took place in the locality known as Nad mlynom. It is precisely from this locality that the most extensive assemblage of archaeological finds from many periods is available. That is also why we can boldly call it a “chronicle of the distant past of the region”. In 1969–1980 Titus Kolník investigated at Cífer-Pác a remarkable building complex dated to the 4th century. A central square precinct measuring about 60 × 70 m was delimited by a wooden palisade. In the enclosed quadrangular area the main building was represented by a multi-roomed structure with stone foundations and with under-floor heating, the so-called hypocaustum. A second, somewhat smaller building with stone foundations was erected outside the enclosed court. Inside the court stood a further 16 wooden log-built and post-built structures. They were arranged above all along the palisade, with a free space left in the middle. Some of the wooden buildings were provided with projecting colonnades – porticoes. The mutual relationships of the individual ground plans testify to at least three phases of construction. In the immediate vicinity of the enclosed area there was an economic and production precinct. Part of it was investigated to the east and to the north of the court.

blocks.caption: The exhibitions in the Cífer - Pác archaeopark
blocks.alt: The exhibitions in the Cífer - Pác archaeopark

children.text: It was represented above all by semi-sunken buildings with the characteristic “Quadic” six-post scheme. Two features of exceptionally large dimensions attract particular attention. They had wooden roof frames covered with Roman roof tiles. Dozens of clay loom weights were found on their floors, which prove that they served as weaving workshops. There were also two wells and three pottery kilns here. A third well was inside the enclosed court.

In this small archaeopark two cultural phenomena of that period – the Roman and the Germanic – are presented side by side, on the example of the Germanic hamlet and the magnate’s court at Cífer-Pác. Cultural events and interesting lectures also add to the appeal of the archaeopark. The kind lady at the ticket desk in the archaeopark also recommended a walk along the educational trail which runs practically from the entrance gate of the archaeopark towards the observation tower.

children.text: We rounded off this pleasant and instructive trip around ancient monuments over a single weekend at the swimming pool right next to the archaeopark in Cífer… after all, the Romans too were fond of baths.

Roman camps, also known as “castra”, were key defensive and logistical structures on the frontiers of the Roman Empire. The distribution of these camps depended on several factors, including geographical conditions, strategic aims and the availability of resources. On the frontiers the camps were usually placed about 30–40 km apart, which is the distance of one day’s march. On the Danube frontier these camps were not always within sight of one another, and the existence of small defensive forts distributed along the Danube between the stone camps in the meanders of the river can therefore be assumed. These centres were linked by a road which did not always follow the course of the river. In some places the bank of the Danube was difficult to pass, so the road ran further into the interior of the province. This network of roads, known as the Viae Romanae, made rapid transport, the movement of troops and supply possible. Where it was possible the road ran along the Danube, and the camps were built so that, from the point of view of defence, it was possible to see from one to the next.

If we look at the distance between the city of Carnuntum and Brigetio, we realise that it is about 85 km, so that works out at two days’ march. Between these two cities there are two important Roman camps: Ad Flexum near the present-day town of Mosonmagyaróvár on the bank of the river Leitha, and a second camp named Arrabona. Arrabona lies near the present-day town of Győr and controlled the crossing of the Danube. On the Slovak side of the Danube we should also not forget the camp of Gerulata in Rusovce.
If you like history, then we can only recommend this circuit in the Hungarian–Slovak–Austrian border region, which we travelled a few days ago with our children.
